Front: What defines a non-periodic signal, and what is a chirp?
Back: Its frequency components change over time (no single fixed spectrum), unlike a periodic signal with one constant spectrum. A chirp is the canonical example: a signal whose frequency sweeps/varies over time.

Front: Relationship between frequency and phase; how do you build a chirp?
Back: Frequency is the derivative of phase; phase is the integral of frequency. Constant frequency -> linear phase (phi = 2*pi*f*t). For a chirp, f varies, so integrate f(t) to get phi(t) then take sin(phi). Instantaneous frequency = slope of phase.

Front: What is the STFT and what does a spectrogram show?
Back: STFT: chop the signal into short (windowed, often overlapping) segments and take the DFT of each, showing how the spectrum evolves over time. Spectrogram visualizes it: x=time, y=frequency, color=amplitude. A chirp appears as a diagonal streak.

Front: Time resolution vs frequency resolution formulas (segment length n, frame rate r)?
Back: Time resolution = n/r; frequency resolution = r/n (reciprocals). A longer segment (bigger n) gives finer frequency resolution but coarser time resolution.

You cannot be precise in time AND frequency at once. A short segment pinpoints WHEN but blurs WHAT frequency; a long segment nails frequency but blurs when. Buying frequency detail costs time detail (and vice versa).

The DFT assumes the segment is one period of a repeating signal. If the end does not connect smoothly to the start, the discontinuity injects spurious frequencies - energy leaks into neighboring frequency bins.

Front: How does windowing fix leakage, and name a common window?
Back: Multiply the segment element-wise by a window that tapers amplitude to ~zero at both edges, removing the discontinuity when the DFT loops it. Hamming is common (Hann, Blackman are cousins). Trade-off: less leakage but a slightly wider main peak.

Front: Distinguish white, pink, and Brownian noise; how is Gaussian different?
Back: Spectrum shapes: white = equal power at all frequencies; pink = power ~ 1/f; Brownian/red = random walk (value = prev + step), power ~ 1/f^2. Gaussian is a different descriptor - the amplitude DISTRIBUTION (bell curve), not the spectrum. They are independent (e.g. Gaussian white noise).
